title: Time Is a Direction Too
question: Why do physicists treat time as a fourth dimension?
hook: Your clock, it turns out, is only one observer's opinion.
idea: Space and time combine into one four-dimensional spacetime, and an object's passage through it depends on how it moves.

beats.prompt: A traveler flies past you at very high speed. According to special relativity, how does time pass for her as you measure it?

choices.label: Exactly as fast as for you, since time is universal
choices.feedback: This is the older classical view, where time is the same for everyone, but special relativity replaces it.

choices.label: At a rate that depends on her velocity relative to you
It stops entirely whenever she moves at all
choices.feedback: Motion changes the observed rate, but nothing in the sentences says it halts.

beats.explain: The observed rate at which time passes depends on the object's velocity relative to the observer.

beats.prompt: match each term to its meaning
pairs: A single point in spacetime, set by x, y, z and t
A particle's path as a sequence of events
The 1908 four-dimensional fusion of space and time
beats.explain: Each term describes a piece of the four-dimensional picture: points, paths and the whole arena.

beats.prompt: sort each idea into its group
items: Time passes at the same rate for every observer
Gravity can slow time as seen from outside
beats.explain: Classical mechanics keeps time universal and separate; relativity ties time to motion and gravity.

beats.prompt: one step in this reasoning is wrong; which?
steps: An event is a single point in spacetime, set by x, y, z and t.
Mathematical events have zero duration, unlike a firecracker's pop.
So an observer can be in motion relative to an event, just as to a firecracker.
beats.explain: You can move relative to a firecracker, but not relative to a mathematical event, which is just a point.
